title: Heckel-clarina
builder: none yet (once ranged: a sound-alike of soprano saxophone by parent rule 1, unless the controller rules Schlesinger's register timbre a trait the build cannot make, then its own build)
notes: A hand-off: batch-14.tsv DROP (family clarinets, hs 422.212): «Belongs to saxophones (H-S 422.212): 'The heckel-clarina is a [[Single-reed instrument|single reed]], conical [[bore (wind instruments)|bore]] instrument made of metal, resembling a [[soprano saxophone]].'». Decided here. Heckel-clarina page (raw wikitext https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Heckel-clarina&action=raw, saved as build/batch-19-pages/heckel-clarina--1.txt): «The heckel-clarina is a [[Single-reed instrument|single reed]], conical [[bore (wind instruments)|bore]] instrument made of metal, resembling a [[soprano saxophone]].» (cited to Dullat 2001, a German book not reached online). Boundary ruling 1: a single reed on a conical bore, so this family, with the class those words imply, 422.212 (the Hornbostel-Sachs aerophone list, raw wikitext https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_aerophones_by_Hornbostel%E2%80%93Sachs_number&action=raw, saved as heckel-clarina--3.txt: «422.212 With conical bore.»). The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article «Clarina» by Kathleen Schlesinger, cited by the page (Wikisource's transcription, raw wikitext https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Page:EB1911_-_Volume_06.djvu/453&action=raw, saved as heckel-clarina--2.txt; the article page 1911_Encyclopædia_Britannica/Clarina only transcludes it): «The clarina is a metal instrument with the conical bore and fingering of the oboe and the clarinet single-reed mouthpiece.» Not a one-off: its maker, Heckel (https://heckel.de/en/the-company/, raw HTML saved as heckel-clarina--4.txt): «Heckel produced many other woodwind instruments such as clarinets, clarinas, oboes, flutes, basset horns (alto clarinet) and English horns.»; the page: «Heckel received a patent for the instrument on 8 December 1889.» Its other names on the page («also known as ''clarina'' or ''patent clarina''») are no audit name. Range (checked first): the page's «Two versions were available: a sopranino in E-flat and a soprano in B-flat.» gives two sizes and calls neither standard (range ruling 6), and its «The range of the B♭ instrument is:» is followed by two images, «[[File:Britannica Clarina Notation.jpg]]» and «[[File:Britannica Clarina Real Sounds.jpg]]», a chart (range ruling 5) for one size only (ruling 4b). Schlesinger's article: «The compass of the instrument is as shown, and it stands in the key of B♭.» (the same two images: a chart) and «Like the clarinet, the clarina is a transposing instrument, for which the music must be written in a key a tone higher than that of the composition.» (a transposition with no notes, ruling 5). No fetched source names the notes, so WAIT a sourced range. Engine limit, once ranged: Schlesinger states a bore effect on the sound: «The timbre resulting from the combination of conical bore and single-reed mouthpiece has in the lowest register affinities with the ''cor anglais'', in the middle with the saxophone, and in the highest with the clarinet.» (the page repeats it from Heckel's promotional materials, cited to Dullat: «the heckel-clarina's tone resembled that of a [[cor anglais]] in its low [[register (music)|register]], a [[saxophone]] in the middle, and a [[clarinet]] in its upper range.»). A timbre that changes by register is a series that changes with the note, which no builder makes, and the bore is named as its cause, so it is reported to the controller under the SHIP ruling; unless the controller rules it colour words, it would wait for its own build (a timbre that changes by register) once ranged. Parent once ranged (rule 1): «resembling a [[soprano saxophone]]» relates the instrument as a whole, the soprano saxophone being a catalog entry (Ab3 to Eb6).

notes: Sound-alike: a hand-off, batch-14.tsv DROP (family clarinets, hs 422.212): «Belongs to saxophones (H-S 422.212): 'Despite its name, it is essentially a wooden [[saxophone]] with wide conical [[bore (wind instruments)|bore]]», decided here. Heckelphone-clarinet page (raw wikitext https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Heckelphone-clarinet&action=raw, saved as build/batch-19-pages/heckelphone-clarinet--1.txt), cited to Dullat 2001 (not reached online): «Despite its name, it is essentially a wooden [[saxophone]] with wide conical [[bore (wind instruments)|bore]], built of red-stained maple wood, [[overblowing]] the octave, and with [[clarinet]]-like fingerings.» and «It has a [[Single-reed instrument|single-reed]] [[mouthpiece (woodwind)|mouthpiece]] attached to a short metal neck, similar to an [[alto clarinet]].» Reed and bore: a single reed on a wide conical bore, boundary ruling 1, so this family and 422.212 (the Hornbostel-Sachs aerophone list, raw wikitext https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_aerophones_by_Hornbostel%E2%80%93Sachs_number&action=raw, saved as heckelphone-clarinet--2.txt: «422.212 With conical bore.»). A production instrument of one maker, not a one-off: «only between twelve and fifteen were manufactured». Its sound: «The instrument sounds somewhat like a saxophone, but with a much softer tone.» and Heckel's 1931 catalogue, quoted on the page: «the clarinet-like tone of the instrument is excellent, extraordinarily harmonious, and powerful; nor is it sharp or metallic like that of the alto saxophone».: colour words, no trait (rule 7). A wood body, maple, the clarinet-like fingering and the metal neck are a material, keywork and a part, no trait; the «wide conical bore» is named, but no fetched source states its effect on the sound, so it is no trait the SHIP ruling holds (noted for the controller). So a sound-alike, builder unchanged. Parent (rule 2): «essentially a wooden [[saxophone]]» names `saxophone`, which is neither a catalog name nor an alias, and Heckel's «nor is it sharp or metallic like that of the alto saxophone» contrasts the two, relating no instrument; so the catalog saxophone whose lowest note is nearest D3: alto saxophone Db3 is 1 semitone away (c melody saxophone Bb2 is 4, soprano saxophone Ab3 and tenor saxophone Ab2 are 6), so alto saxophone. The alto saxophone is a catalog entry from before the batch (D♭3 to A♭5; the catalog's saxophones carry no per-entry source). Range: the page, cited to Marcuse, Musical Instruments: A Comprehensive Dictionary (1975; every archive.org copy is access-restricted and its search-inside refused curl with a 403, so the cited work was not reached): «The heckelphone-clarinet is a [[transposing instrument]] in B{{music|flat}} with sounding range of D<sub>3</sub> (middle line of bass staff) to C<sub>6</sub> (two ledger lines above the treble staff), written a whole tone higher.» A sounding range, both notes from one source, taken as given (range rulings 1 and 2): D3 to C6, inside A0 to C8 (written E3 to D6, a whole tone higher, as the same sentence says).

A production type, not a one-off: «It was later patented in 1893 by Oskar Adler and Hermann Jordan of [[Markneukirchen]], Germany.» Range (checked first): the page's «The (written) range of the octavin is from G♯<sub>3</sub> to G<sub>6</sub>.» is written with no transposition (range ruling 2), and its citation, the Hartenberger World Musical Instrument Collection's «Octavin-Bb: 'Adler & Co.'» (https://wmic.net/octavin-bb-adler-co/, raw HTML saved as octavin--2.txt), gives no such range: it says only «There are 14 touch pieces and 3 rings, with a playable range up to the (written) C#.» (one letter with no octave, ruling 5), so the line is uncited (ruling 10: a citation that gives no range is none). Parent once ranged (rule 1): the Horniman's page quotes Langwill: «has a tone somewhat like that of the soprano saxophone but less pleasant», a museum relating the whole instrument's sound to a catalog entry (the page's «The octavin resembles a [[saxophone]]» names no catalog entry).

name: tarogato
title: Tárogató
notes: DROP: an ambiguous name: the modern single-reed tárogató (Schunda's, 1890s) and the historical double-reed tárogató it was made to recreate. A hand-off: batch-14.tsv DROP (family clarinets, hs 422.212): «Belongs to saxophones (H-S 422.212): the modern instrument 'uses a single reed, like a [[clarinet]] or [[saxophone]], and has a [[conical bore]], similar to the saxophone.'», decided here by the ambiguous ruling first. Tárogató page (raw wikitext https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=T%C3%A1rogat%C3%B3&action=raw, saved as build/batch-19-pages/tarogato--1.txt): «The modern tárogató was intended to be a recreation of the original tárogató, which was historically a synonym for the toröksip (“Turkish pipe”) or [[zurna]].» and «Up to around the 18th century, the tárogató had a [[double reed]], [[conical bore]], and no [[Key (instrument)|keys]].» and «The modern tárogató bears very little resemblance to the historical tárogató and the two instruments should not be confused.», each cited to Stephen Fox, a clarinet and tárogató maker, whose article «The Tárogató» (http://www.sfoxclarinets.com/Tarogatoart.html, raw HTML saved as tarogato--2.txt) says: «of the present day bears very little resemblance to the instrument bearing the same name in earlier times.» and «Before the mid 19th century, the term referred to keyless, conical bored, double reed instruments - shawms, generically speaking -». The page's «However, the táragató and töroksip/zurna are today considered to be distinct instruments.» separates the zurna, not the old tárogató: the page still calls that one «the original tárogató» and «the historical tárogató», so the sources give the name to two instruments, past and present (the ambiguous ruling; a later pass may add `modern tarogato`). Its infobox «names = {{hlist|Taragot|töröksíp|torogoata|Turkish pipe}}» does not outweigh the text (the names ruling), and none of them is an audit name. The page gives no class (hs none); the aerophone list's «[[Tarogato]] (modern)» is the modern one's. Ranges on the saved pages, for the later pass: the infobox's «Written range: B{{flat}}<sub>3</sub> to C<sub>6</sub> ([[scientific pitch notation]])» has no `<ref>` and no transposition in its field (range rulings 2 and 10); Fox's «and a range down to low Bb» is a letter with no octave (ruling 5); sizes: «The most common size, the soprano tárogató in B{{Flat}}, is around {{Convert|74|cm|in}} in length», «Other sizes exist: one maker, János Stowasser, advertised a family of seven sizes of which the largest was a contrabass tárogató in E{{Flat}}.» and Fox's «in Bb is and has always been by far the most common type» (ruling 6 would let a source's range for the B♭ soprano range a `modern tarogato` row; none of the saved pages gives one). Parent leads for that pass: «It uses a single reed, like a [[clarinet]] or [[saxophone]]» compares the reed (no rule 1); Fox's «The new tárogató could be roughly described as a soprano saxophone» relates the whole instrument to a catalog entry.
